questions.question: What does the abbreviation ASCII stand for?

options.text: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
American Scientific Code for Internet Integration
Advanced System for Computer Input and Integration
Automatic System for Coding Interactive Interfaces

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**American Standard Code for Information Interchange**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **ASCII** stands for **American Standard Code for Information Interchange**. It is a character encoding standard used in computers and electronic devices.
 
• ASCII was developed in **1963** by the American National Standards Institute (**ANSI**), primarily for the representation of English characters and symbols in digital systems.
 
• The ASCII code consists of **128 characters**, including **control characters** (0–31), printable characters (32–127), numbers, uppercase and lowercase letters, and special symbols.
 
• ASCII is widely used in computer systems for text processing, communication protocols, and file formats. It provides a standardized way to represent and transfer textual data.
 
• The ASCII standard ensures compatibility across various devices and platforms, making it a foundational element in computer science and digital communication.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Control Characters in ASCII:**

 
 
• Control characters (0–31) are non-printable and used for specific functions like **formatting** or **device control**. Examples include **carriage return (CR)**, **line feed (LF)**, and **escape (ESC)**.
 
• These characters are essential for managing data transmission and communication protocols.
 
 
 
• **Printable Characters in ASCII:**
 
 
• Printable characters range from 32 to 127 and include **letters**, **digits**, **punctuation marks**, and **special symbols**.
 
• Examples: **A-Z**, **0-9**, **!**, **@**, **#**, and **$**.
 
 
 
• **Extended ASCII:**
 
 
• Extended ASCII includes an additional **128 characters** (128–255) for representing international symbols, graphical characters, and additional mathematical symbols.
 
• It is commonly used in systems supporting languages beyond English.
 
 
 
• **Applications of ASCII:**
 
 
• ASCII is extensively used in **file formats**, such as **.txt**, **.csv**, and **HTML**.
 
• It is a fundamental standard for **network communication protocols** like HTTP and SMTP.
 
• ASCII also plays a key role in **programming**, data storage, and text processing systems.
 
 
 
• **Evolution and Alternatives:**
 
 
• ASCII served as the foundation for modern character encoding standards like **Unicode**, which supports a wider range of characters from different languages.
 
• Unicode is backward compatible with ASCII, ensuring seamless integration in global systems.

questions.question: Which of the following dynasties initiated the practice of land grants to Brahmanas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Satavahanas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Satavahana dynasty** is credited with initiating the practice of **land grants** to Brahmanas (Brahmins) and religious institutions.
 
• This tradition of land grants, also known as **brahmadeya**, started during the rule of the Satavahanas in ancient India and became a notable feature of Indian polity and economy in later periods.
 
• The grants were generally given to Brahmanas for performing **Vedic rituals** and maintaining religious and educational institutions.
 
• These land grants were typically recorded in inscriptions, and the beneficiaries were often exempted from taxes and other obligations.
 
• The Satavahanas used these grants as a means to consolidate their political power and gain the support of the Brahmin class, which held significant social and religious influence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Satavahana Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Satavahanas ruled parts of central and southern India from the **1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE**.
 
• Their capital cities included **Pratishthana (modern Paithan)** and Amaravati.
 
• The dynasty played a crucial role in promoting **Buddhism** and **Brahmanism** simultaneously, reflecting religious tolerance.
 
• Prominent rulers included **Gautamiputra Satakarni** and **Vashishtiputra Pulumavi**.
 
 
 
• **Land Grants in Indian History:**
 
 
• The practice of granting land to Brahmanas started with the Satavahanas and was later adopted by dynasties like the Guptas and Cholas.
 
• Such grants were often made in perpetuity, and the beneficiaries had the right to collect taxes from the land.
 
• These grants contributed to the development of **agrarian economies** and the spread of **Brahmanical culture**.
 
 
 
• **Other Dynasties Mentioned in the Question:**
 
 
• **Kushanas:** Known for their patronage of Buddhism and the **Silk Road trade**, the Kushanas ruled during the 1st-3rd centuries CE. However, they are not associated with initiating land grants.
 
• **Cholas:** The Cholas, especially in the medieval period, extensively granted land to temples and Brahmins. However, they adopted the tradition much later than the Satavahanas.
 
• **Guptas:** Known as the "Golden Age of India," the Gupta Empire also issued land grants, but this practice gained prominence after the Satavahana period.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Brahmadeya Grants:**
 
 
• These grants facilitated the spread of **Brahmanical culture** and religious practices in rural areas.
 
• They helped in integrating local communities into the larger political framework of the ruling dynasty.

questions.question: Which islands of India are strategically important due to their location near the Malacca Strait?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andaman and Nicobar Islands**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** are strategically located near the **Malacca Strait**, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world.
 
• The **Malacca Strait** is a crucial maritime passage that connects the **Indian Ocean** to the **South China Sea** and the **Pacific Ocean**, making it a vital route for global trade.
 
• India’s control over the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** enhances its ability to monitor and secure this critical sea lane, which is essential for energy and trade flow between countries like China, Japan, and Southeast Asia.
 
• The islands are home to the **Tri-services Command** of the Indian armed forces, the only joint command in India, allowing for coordinated defense operations in the region.
 
• Due to their proximity to Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, the islands act as a critical outpost for ensuring maritime security, combating piracy, and asserting India’s presence in the Indo-Pacific region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Andaman and Nicobar Islands:**

 
 
• Located in the **Bay of Bengal**, these islands comprise 572 islands, of which only about 37 are inhabited.
 
• The islands span an area of approximately **8,249 square kilometers** and have immense ecological and geopolitical significance.
 
• The **Indira Point**, located on Great Nicobar Island, is the southernmost point of India.
 
• The islands support India’s strategic interests in the **Indo-Pacific region** and act as a natural barrier to shipping routes.
 
 
 
• **Malacca Strait:**
 
 
• The **Malacca Strait** is a narrow stretch of water between the **Malay Peninsula** and the Indonesian island of **Sumatra**.
 
• It is one of the busiest shipping lanes globally, with about **25% of the world’s traded goods** passing through it annually.
 
• The strait is especially crucial for countries like **China** and **Japan**, which depend heavily on imported oil transported through this route.
 
• The strategic importance of the strait makes it a potential hotspot for geopolitical tensions and maritime piracy.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Andaman and Nicobar Islands for India:**
 
 
• The islands are equipped with naval bases and airstrips, enabling India to monitor activities in the **Indian Ocean** and the **South China Sea**.
 
• India has plans to further develop the islands under the **Act East Policy** to improve maritime connectivity with Southeast Asia.
 
• The islands play a crucial role in disaster management and humanitarian assistance missions in the region.
 
 
 
• **Other Island Groups of India:**
 
 
• **Gulf of Kutch Islands:** Located in Gujarat, these islands are not strategically close to the Malacca Strait but are significant for marine biodiversity and oil exploration.
 
• **Lakshadweep Islands:** Situated in the Arabian Sea, these islands are significant for India’s western maritime boundary but are not near the Malacca Strait.
 
• **Rameswaram Islands:** Located in Tamil Nadu, these islands are closer to Sri Lanka and are important for religious tourism and local fishing activities.

questions.question: How did globalisation affect India’s economic growth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Made it grow faster**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Globalisation** has significantly contributed to **India's economic growth** by fostering integration with the global economy, boosting trade, and encouraging investment.
 
• India adopted the **Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG)** model in **1991**, which opened up various sectors to foreign investment and competition, leading to a surge in **economic activities**.
 
• The **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** of India witnessed a steady growth trajectory post-globalisation. In the 1990s, the GDP growth rate averaged around **5.5%**, and it increased to over **7%** in the 2000s.
 
• Globalisation attracted **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** in key sectors like technology, manufacturing, and services. For example, FDI inflows into India increased from **$129 million in 1991** to **$67 billion in 2020**.
 
• Globalisation also led to the rise of the **IT and software services sector** in India, with companies like **Infosys, TCS, and Wipro** becoming global players. This sector is now a major contributor to India's GDP and exports.
 
• India's participation in global markets also boosted exports of goods and services, which increased from **$18 billion in 1991** to over **$400 billion in 2023**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Impact of Globalisation on Various Sectors:**

 
 
• **Agriculture:** Globalisation introduced modern farming techniques and equipment, improving productivity. However, it also led to challenges like dependency on imports for fertilizers and seeds.
 
• **Manufacturing:** The "Make in India" initiative was launched to attract global manufacturers. This sector benefited from FDI and technological advancements.
 
• **Services:** The IT and outsourcing industry flourished due to global demand for software and customer service. India became a hub for **Business Process Outsourcing (BPO).**
 
 
 
• **Key Reforms During Globalisation in India:**
 
 
• **Industrial Policy of 1991:** Reduced licensing requirements and restrictions on private sector participation.
 
• **Foreign Trade Policy:** Encouraged exports and reduced import duties to facilitate trade.
 
• **Banking Reforms:** Allowed private and foreign banks to operate in India, increasing competition.
 
 
 
• **Challenges of Globalisation:**
 
 
• **Income Inequality:** While urban areas saw rapid development, rural areas often lagged behind.
 
• **Environmental Concerns:** Industrialisation led to increased pollution and resource depletion.
 
• **Dependency:** Over-reliance on foreign technology and investment made certain sectors vulnerable to global economic fluctuations.
 
 
 
• **Economic Milestones Post-Globalisation:**
 
 
• The **IT revolution** put India on the global map as a technology hub.
 
• Introduction of the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** streamlined taxation and improved ease of doing business.
 
• The **Start-up India initiative** encouraged innovation and entrepreneurship, making India the third-largest start-up ecosystem globally.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Important Indicators of Growth:**

 
 
• **Human Development Index (HDI):** India's HDI improved significantly post-1991, reflecting better life expectancy, education, and standard of living.
 
• **Ease of Doing Business:** India climbed from **142nd position in 2014** to **63rd in 2020** in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business rankings.
 
• **Exports:** Key export items include **textiles, pharmaceuticals, and software services**, contributing to India's foreign exchange reserves.
 
 
 
• **Global Partnerships:**
 
 
• India became a member of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** in 1995, expanding trade opportunities.
 
• Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with countries like **ASEAN, Japan, and South Korea** facilitated market access.

questions.question: Which of the following foods is a source of animal protein?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Eggs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Eggs** are a rich source of **animal protein**, which contains all nine essential amino acids required by the human body for muscle repair, enzyme function, and overall growth.
 
• Animal proteins, such as those found in eggs, are known for their **high biological value**, meaning they provide all essential nutrients in the right proportions.
 
• Eggs are also packed with other key nutrients, including **vitamin B12, selenium, phosphorus, and riboflavin**, which are vital for maintaining healthy bodily functions.
 
• Unlike plant-based proteins (e.g., pulses and beans), eggs contain **complete protein**, making them an excellent choice for meeting daily protein requirements.
 
• Eggs are widely consumed globally due to their nutritional profile and versatility in cooking, making them a common part of diets across different cultures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pulses:**

 
 
• Pulses, such as lentils and chickpeas, are excellent sources of **plant-based protein** but lack one or more essential amino acids, making them incomplete proteins.
 
• They are high in dietary fiber and low in fat, contributing to heart health and digestion.
 
 
 
• **Beans:**
 
 
• Beans, including kidney beans and black beans, are another rich source of **plant protein**, iron, and folate.
 
• While beans are nutritious, they do not contain all essential amino acids required by the human body.
 
 
 
• **Nuts:**
 
 
• Nuts like almonds and walnuts are known for their healthy fats, including **omega-3 fatty acids**, but they are not significant sources of complete protein.
 
• Nuts are commonly consumed as snacks or added to recipes for their nutritional benefits and flavor.
 
 
 
• **Animal Protein:**
 
 
• Animal protein sources include eggs, meat, fish, and dairy products, all of which are **complete proteins**.
 
• Animal protein is essential for individuals with increased protein requirements, such as athletes and pregnant women.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Protein:**
 
 
• Proteins are vital for **cell repair, enzyme production, and hormonal balance**.
 
• A balanced intake of protein, including both plant and animal sources, is recommended for optimal health.

questions.question: Which physical feature acts as a barrier to the southwest monsoon winds, causing heavy rainfall on one side and dry conditions on the other?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Western Ghats**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Western Ghats**, also known as the Sahyadri Hills, run parallel to the western coast of India, covering states like Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.
 
• The range intercepts the **southwest monsoon winds**, causing orographic rainfall on the windward side (western slopes), resulting in heavy rainfall.
 
• The leeward side (eastern slopes) of the Western Ghats experiences a **rain shadow effect**, leading to dry conditions in regions like the Deccan Plateau.
 
• This geographical feature plays a critical role in shaping the climate and biodiversity of the western coastal plains and the adjacent areas.
 
• The dense forests and unique ecology of the Western Ghats have earned it the status of a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** due to its rich biodiversity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Aravalli Range:**

 
 
• Located in the northwestern part of India, the **Aravalli Range** is one of the oldest mountain ranges in the world.
 
• It runs through Rajasthan, Haryana, and Gujarat, and does not significantly impact the monsoon winds.
 
• Unlike the Western Ghats, it is oriented in a northeast-southwest direction, parallel to the monsoon winds, offering no significant barrier effect.
 
 
 
• **Vindhya Range:**
 
 
• The **Vindhya Range** lies in central India and forms a natural divide between northern and southern India.
 
• It does not have a significant impact on monsoon winds as it is not located in the path of the southwest monsoon.
 
 
 
• **Satpura Range:**
 
 
• The **Satpura Range** lies to the south of the Vindhya Range in central India, separating the northern plains from the Deccan Plateau.
 
• Although it influences local climatic patterns, it does not significantly impact the southwest monsoon winds like the Western Ghats.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Western Ghats:**
 
 
• The Western Ghats are home to several important rivers such as the **Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri**, which originate from its slopes.
 
• They are a biodiversity hotspot, hosting a variety of endemic flora and fauna.
 
• The heavy rainfall supports dense forests, agriculture, and hydropower projects in the region.

questions.question: Which of the following Amendments made Education a subject in the Concurrent List?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**42nd Amendment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act** of the Indian Constitution, enacted in **1976**, is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" due to its extensive modifications to the Constitution.
 
• This amendment transferred **Education** from the **State List** to the **Concurrent List**, allowing both the Union and State governments to legislate on education matters.
 
• The aim of this transfer was to ensure **uniformity in education policies** across the country and improve the quality of education nationwide.
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act also introduced significant changes in the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, and Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs).
 
• This amendment was passed during the **Emergency period** under the leadership of then-Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Concurrent List:**

 
 
• The Concurrent List is one of the three lists in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution, along with the Union List and State List.
 
• Subjects in the Concurrent List allow both the **Central** and **State governments** to legislate. In case of conflict, the Union law prevails.
 
• Examples of subjects in the Concurrent List include **education, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, and trade unions**.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act Overview:**
 
 
• It introduced concepts like the **Fundamental Duties** under Article 51A and emphasized the Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
• It also extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies from **5 years to 6 years** (later reverted by the 44th Amendment).
 
• The amendment aimed at promoting a **socialist, secular, and integrity-driven nation** by altering the Preamble.
 
 
 
• **Education in India:**
 
 
• Initially a State subject, education was brought into the Concurrent List to improve **uniformity and quality standards** across the nation.
 
• Post the 42nd Amendment, major educational initiatives like the **Right to Education Act (RTE), Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan,** and National Education Policies were undertaken by the Union Government.
 
 
 
• **Other Amendments Related to Education:**
 
 
• The **86th Amendment Act, 2002**, made education a Fundamental Right under Article 21A for children aged **6 to 14 years**.
 
• The **93rd Amendment Act, 2005**, allowed reservations for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in educational institutions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Concurrent List Subjects:**

 
 
• Subjects like **criminal law, forests, economic and social planning, and education** are part of the Concurrent List.
 
• The inclusion of education in the Concurrent List strengthened **policy coordination between the Centre and States**.
 
 
 
• **Impact of 42nd Amendment:**
 
 
• This amendment is considered a landmark in Indian constitutional history as it significantly strengthened the role of the Union government.
 
• It also faced criticism for being passed during the **Emergency period**, when democratic functioning was heavily restricted.

questions.question: Which of the following falls under the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction, according to the Constitution of India (Article 131)?

options.text: Appeals from criminal cases in High Courts
Disputes between States or between a State and the Union
Enforcement of fundamental rights of individuals
Election petitions against sitting Members of Parliaments

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Disputes between States or between a State and the Union**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 131** of the **Constitution of India** provides for the **original jurisdiction** of the **Supreme Court**. This jurisdiction is invoked in disputes between the **States** or between a **State** and the **Union Government**.
 
• Under this article, the Supreme Court acts as the arbitrator in case of legal disputes or conflicts between governments within India. ***Hence, this is the correct option.***
 
• Appeals from criminal cases in High Courts fall under the **appellate jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court, not its original jurisdiction. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• The enforcement of fundamental rights is under the **writ jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court (Article 32) and not its original jurisdiction. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• Election petitions against sitting Members of Parliament are adjudicated by the **High Courts** and do not fall under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court:**

 
 
• The original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is defined under **Article 131** of the Constitution of India.
 
• It primarily deals with disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between two or more States.
 
• Examples include disputes over water sharing, territorial boundaries, and constitutional matters.
 
• This jurisdiction ensures the resolution of inter-governmental conflicts through a single, neutral judicial body.
 
 
 
• **Appellate Jurisdiction:**
 
 
• Under its appellate jurisdiction, the Supreme Court hears appeals against judgments from lower courts, including the High Courts.
 
• This includes appeals in criminal cases, civil disputes, and constitutional matters.
 
• The appellate jurisdiction is governed by **Articles 132 to 134** of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Writ Jurisdiction (Article 32):**
 
 
• The Supreme Court has the authority to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
 
• This jurisdiction is often termed as the "guardian of fundamental rights" and is fundamental to the functioning of the judiciary in India.
 
• The writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari.
 
 
 
• **Election Petitions:**
 
 
• Election petitions are filed in the High Courts under the **Representation of the People Act, 1951**.
 
• The Supreme Court does not have original jurisdiction in election matters; it can only hear appeals arising from High Court judgments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Examples of Original Jurisdiction:**

 
 
• **State Water Disputes:** Disputes over water sharing between States, such as the **Cauvery Water Dispute**.
 
• **Boundary Disputes:** Conflicts over territorial boundaries between States like Maharashtra and Karnataka.
 
 
 
• **Limitations:**
 
 
• The original jurisdiction does not apply to private individuals or entities.
 
• It is limited to inter-governmental disputes as defined under Article 131.

questions.question: Which law explains the colours of black bodies including the Sun and other stars in terms of their temperatures?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Wien's Displacement Law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Wien's Displacement Law** explains the relationship between the temperature of a black body and the wavelength at which it emits radiation most strongly.
 
• It states that the wavelength corresponding to the peak emission of radiation is inversely proportional to the temperature of the black body. **Mathematically, λ_max = b/T**, where **λ_max** is the peak wavelength, **T** is the temperature, and **b** is Wien's constant (approximately **2.897 × 10⁻³ m·K**).
 
• This law helps us understand the colors emitted by black bodies like stars, including the **Sun**, based on their surface temperature. For example, hotter stars emit blue light, while cooler stars emit red light.
 
• The law was formulated by **Wilhelm Wien** in **1893** and is a fundamental concept in **thermodynamics and astrophysics**.
 
• It is widely applied in determining the temperature of celestial objects by analyzing the spectrum of their emitted radiation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hooke's Law:**

 
 
• Hooke's Law pertains to the **elasticity of materials** and states that the force needed to extend or compress a spring is proportional to the distance it is stretched or compressed (**F = kx**, where **k** is the spring constant).
 
• It is unrelated to black body radiation or temperature.
 
 
 
• **Snell's Law:**
 
 
• Snell's Law describes the **refraction of light** as it passes from one medium to another, stating that the ratio of the sine of the angles of incidence and refraction is proportional to the refractive indices of the media (**n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂**).
 
• This law is used in optics and is not related to the emission of radiation by black bodies.
 
 
 
• **Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion:**
 
 
• These laws describe the motion of planets around the Sun:
 
• **1st Law:** Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.
 
• **2nd Law:** A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time.
 
• **3rd Law:** The square of the orbital period of a planet is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.
 
• While these laws are significant in celestial mechanics, they do not explain the colors of black bodies based on their temperature.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Wien's Displacement Law** is essential for understanding the spectrum of stars and other celestial objects, allowing scientists to estimate their **surface temperatures**.
 
• The Sun, for example, emits radiation most strongly at a wavelength of approximately **500 nm** (green light), corresponding to its surface temperature of about **5778 K**.
 
• It is a crucial tool in **astrophysics** and helps in the study of **stellar evolution**.

questions.solution:

__
 
• **Macaulay's Minute on Education**, written in **1835**, was a landmark document that proposed the introduction of **English education in India**.
 
• The document was prepared by **Thomas Babington Macaulay**, a member of the Supreme Council of India, and advocated for the replacement of traditional Indian education systems with an English-based education system.
 
• It aimed to create a class of Indians who would act as intermediaries between the British rulers and the Indian masses, often referred to as "a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect."
 
• The policy led to the establishment of **English-medium schools** and the promotion of English as the medium of instruction for higher education in India.
 
• This initiative had a lasting impact on Indian education and society, making English a prominent language in India to this day.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Regulating Act (1773):**

 
 
• The **Regulating Act of 1773** was the first step towards the centralization of administration in British India, but it had no specific focus on education.
 
• The act aimed to address corruption in the East India Company and improve governance, particularly in Bengal.
 
 
 
• **Pitt's India Act (1784):**
 
 
• The **Pitt's India Act** created a dual system of control for British India, dividing power between the East India Company and the British Crown.
 
• Like the Regulating Act, it had no provisions or policies related to education.
 
 
 
• **Charter Act of 1813:**
 
 
• The **Charter Act of 1813** was the first significant legislation to recognize the importance of education in India.
 
• It allocated a sum of **₹1 lakh** annually for the promotion of education, marking the beginning of state-sponsored education in India.
 
• However, it lacked clear direction on the medium of instruction, which was later clarified by Macaulay's Minute.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Macaulay's Minute:**
 
 
• Macaulay's policies led to the establishment of institutions like the **University of Calcutta**, **University of Bombay**, and **University of Madras** in 1857.
 
• It also laid the foundation for the dominance of English in Indian education, administration, and judiciary.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Background:**

 
 
• Before Macaulay's Minute, indigenous education systems in India focused on traditional learning in Sanskrit, Persian, and regional languages.
 
• The British debated whether to promote traditional Indian education or introduce Western-style education.
 
 
 
• **Criticism:**
 
 
• Macaulay's policies were criticized for undermining India's rich educational heritage and prioritizing English over native languages.
 
• Some argued that the policy created a cultural disconnect among Indians.

__
 
• **Sher Shah Suri**, the founder of the Sur Empire, implemented several administrative reforms to strengthen governance.
 
• He divided his empire into administrative units called **Shiqqs**, which were equivalent to **Sarkars** under the Mughal administration.
 
• A **Sarkar** was a larger administrative division during the Mughal period, composed of multiple **Parganas**.
 
• Sher Shah ensured that each **Sarkar** was managed by efficient officers such as **Shiqdar** (law enforcement officer) and **Munsif** (judicial officer).

• **Sher Shah Suri (1486–1545)** was a visionary ruler known for his effective governance and administrative reforms.
 
• He introduced the **Rupiya**, a silver coin, which became the precursor to the modern Indian currency.
 
• He developed an efficient revenue system based on land measurement and improved communication networks by establishing **Grand Trunk Road**, connecting major cities.

• Under the Mughals, the empire was divided into three main administrative units: **Suba**, **Sarkar**, and **Pargana**.
 
• A **Suba** was the largest division and governed by a Subedar, while a **Sarkar** was managed by a Faujdar and a **Pargana** was overseen by smaller officers like the Qanungo.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Administrative Units:**
 
 
• **Suba:** A province or state under the Mughal empire, the largest administrative unit.
 
• **Sarkar:** A division within a Suba, equivalent to the Shiqqs during Sher Shah’s reign.
 
• **Pargana:** A smaller administrative unit within a Sarkar, consisting of villages.
 
• **Mandal:** This term was used in certain regions but not widely adopted in Mughal administration.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Sher Shah’s Administration:**
 
 
• Sher Shah’s reforms were later adopted and refined by the Mughals, influencing governance in India for centuries.
 
• His focus on efficient revenue collection, law enforcement, and infrastructure development laid the groundwork for modern administrative systems.

• The division of the empire into such units ensured better governance, revenue collection, and law enforcement.
 
 
 
• **Influence on Mughal Administration:**
 
 
• The Mughal emperors adopted and expanded Sher Shah’s administrative framework, further dividing Subas into Sarkars and Parganas.
 
• This hierarchical structure allowed for efficient management and control over vast territories.

• The **Deccan Plateau** is a large triangular plateau in southern India that is bordered by the **Western Ghats** on the west and the **Eastern Ghats** on the east.

• The **Young Bengal Movement** was characterized by its emphasis on freedom of thought, individual liberty, and opposition to outdated customs and superstitions in Indian society.
 
• The movement primarily consisted of young, educated Indians who were inspired by the ideas of the **European Enlightenment** and the French Revolution.
 
• Although the movement was short-lived, it laid the foundation for modern ideas of reform, rationalism, and questioning traditional norms in **19th-century Bengal**.

__
 
• The **Ajanta Caves**, located in the **Aurangabad district** of Maharashtra, India, are a group of **30 rock-cut Buddhist cave monuments** that date back to the 2nd century BCE to about 480 CE.

• **Historical Context of Ajanta Caves:**

 
 
• The caves were built in two phases. The first phase occurred during the **Satavahana period** (2nd century BCE to 1st century CE), while the second phase is associated with the **Vakataka dynasty** (5th century CE).
 
• The caves were rediscovered in **1819** by a British officer named **John Smith** during a tiger-hunting expedition.

• The sculptures and architecture reflect a blend of **Hinayana (Theravada)** and **Mahayana Buddhism**.

• At the time of independence, **India's economy was heavily agrarian**, with agriculture being the largest source of employment and income.
 
• Over 70% of the population resided in rural areas, and their primary occupation revolved around farming and related activities.
 
• Due to the **British colonial policies**, industrial development was neglected, leaving agriculture as the dominant sector.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Agriculture:**
 
 
• Indian agriculture faced several challenges, including **low productivity**, the absence of modern techniques, and fragmented land holdings.
 
• The dependence on **monsoon rains** for irrigation made farming highly vulnerable to climatic conditions.
 
• Peasant exploitation under the **Zamindari system** further aggravated the condition of farmers.
 
 
 
• **Economic Contribution:**
 
 
• Agriculture contributed around **50% of India's GDP** at the time of independence, showcasing its importance in the economy.
 
• Post-independence, the government focused on reforms such as the **abolition of the Zamindari system** and the promotion of cooperative farming.
 
 
 
• **Present-Day Scenario:**
 
 
• Currently, the dependence on agriculture has decreased, with **less than 50%** of the population engaged in agricultural activities.
 
• Industrialization, urbanization, and the growth of the service sector have diversified employment opportunities over the decades.

• **Green Revolution:**

 
 
• The **Green Revolution** in the 1960s aimed to improve agricultural productivity through modern techniques, fertilizers, and high-yield variety seeds.
 
• This initiative significantly boosted food grain production, reducing dependence on imports and ensuring food security.
 
 
 
• **Rural Employment Schemes:**
 
 
• The government introduced schemes like **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)** to provide employment opportunities in rural areas.
 
• Such programs help reduce the reliance on agriculture as the sole source of livelihood for rural populations.
